name: Deutsche Grammophon
editorial_article: Deutsche Grammophon (DG) is arguably the most prestigious and historically significant classical music record label in existence. Founded in Hanover, Germany, in 1898 by Emile Berliner—the inventor of the gramophone disc—and his brother Joseph, the company is as old as the recording industry itself. Originally established to produce discs for the London-based Gramophone Company, it quickly established its own identity, evolving into the world's preeminent archive of Western art music. Throughout the 20th century, the label became synonymous with the "Yellow Label" aesthetic and high-fidelity sound, recording legendary conductors such as Herbert von Karajan and Leonard Bernstein, and supporting icons like Anne-Sophie Mutter. \n\nDG's history is inextricably linked to the technological evolution of recorded sound, from its pioneering use of magnetic tape in 1946 to its early adoption of the long-playing (LP) record and the compact disc. While it has navigated tumultuous political history, including the constraints of the Third Reich era and various corporate realignments—eventually becoming part of the Universal Music Group—it has maintained an unwavering focus on the canon of classical music. In the modern era, the label continues to innovate, embracing digital distribution, curated streaming services, and archival initiatives while managing one of the deepest catalogs in music history. It remains the gold standard for orchestral and chamber music recordings, setting the benchmark for performance quality and recording fidelity.
editorial_description: The world's most famous classical music label, known for its iconic 'Yellow Label' and historic archive of the 20th century's greatest performers.
